results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 53 body units' outline summaries match the controlling idea of their aligned spec paragraph, in spec order (p01..p55, including p47, p48 before p46 as the spec orders them). The three introduction callouts match no spec paragraph and are correctly unmatched (null); they are the KEY POINTS / IN THIS CHAPTER callouts the spec's thesis_statement and roadmap place there.

Outliner marked two ideas (place in the order's journey; Eva's no-code order). Judged one idea: Eva's order is the illustration of 'what may be subtracted from that price at checkout' (free shipping is a promotion too), exactly as the spec's p04 controlling idea joins them.

The paragraph carries two ideas: eligibility depends on customer identity (first order by e-mail, the Familiar Stranger), and a paid membership is a customer attribute read as an eligibility condition, backed by two annual reports. The spec's p15 controlling idea itself joins both, and the spec's flow rationale moved the membership sentence here deliberately, so the draft follows its contract; both flow readers (A5, B4) also found the membership aside out of place.
results.quote: A paid membership (Prime-style: a fee for delivery and other benefits, which Amazon's 2025 annual report counts as subscription revenue and Target's describes as a paid membership) is read the same way

results.finding: Outliner marked two ideas (the rule for leaving platform promotions; governance as cheapest fix). Judged one recommendation: when to change arrangement and what to do until then, as the spec's p37 controlling idea states it in one sentence.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: scene to S1/S3, definitions and pieces to S2/S3, stored value to S4, choices and scale stages to S5 (and S1 via governance), in-practice to S6/S1/S3, failures to S1/S3/S4; the conclusion synthesizes S1-S6. No unit wanders off-thesis (local asides such as the IFRIC 13 history are sentence-level and recorded under flow).

Explained: the incident table (three costs, then diagnosed in the next paragraph), Figure 1, the promotion-type table ('Read the last column'), the Ridgewalker margin, Figure 5, the three vendor sources ('One idea, three vendors'), Amazon/Target, Adobe batch codes, the Adobe quotation ('That is why the product page can only show an estimate'), commercetools distribution, the VAT example, Eva's allocation table (refund €179.10; 'the missing step is the Net line price column'), Starbucks figures, the Shopify store-credit quotation, both choice and scale tables, ACM's worked example, Ravelin, Gubela et al., and the 2027 plan table ('Two changes matter more than the table'). One gap recorded separately (p39 €179).

The running-example evidence of p39 (spec: 'the rule applied to the running example') gives a figure without saying where it comes from: the reader is not told what the Price Drift did to the Ridgewalker's price or why €179 is the lowest price of the prior 30 days. Both flow readers could not follow it (A11, B12).
results.quote: Had Kestrel & Pine's Price Drift run into November, the German strike-through price for the Ridgewalker would legally have been €179, not €199.

The intro-only reader predicted every roadmap section in order (Stacking Bug; what a promotion is; five parts and where the final discount is computed; discount to invoice, refund and books with Eva's worked allocation; stored value as ledgers; four options by scale stage; dated examples and the 2027 plan; failure patterns) and the evidence (incident, worked allocation, three platforms' documentation, accounting standards, a company filing), matching the expected answer.

The cold reader computed €179.10, allocated €23.50 in proportion (€19.90 jacket, €3.60 socks) and said the net price per line must be written to the order at order time and carried by the export to the returns tool and ERP, matching the expected answer.

The cold reader named the unowned combination setting not checked against the campaign plan, then gave one owner for the settings, a plan with order of evaluation and stop rule, one calendar and a test against every active promotion in staging, all before any new tool; matches the expected governance-first answer.

The cold reader said a gift card is value paid in advance and owed, a contract liability kept as a ledger, and that finance reconciles the summed balances to the liability account every month; matches expected.

results.draft_locus: In Practice > Dated, sourced examples, paragraph 2 (The prior-price rule turns promotions into a data requirement)
results.quote: For architecture this means an effective-dated price history (each price stored with the dates it applied) per SKU per country that can answer "lowest price in the last 30 days" when a promotion is published, and a strike-through price (the crossed-out earlier price shown beside the reduced one) that is itself a syndicated field.
results.finding: 'Syndicated field' is not explained here or earlier in the chapter and is not on already_knows; a reader new to commerce does not know that syndication means sending product data out to other channels (marketplaces, feeds, stores), so the consequence — that the strike-through price must travel to every channel copy — is lost.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, item A11 ('"Syndicated field" ... is also unexplained jargon')
